name: PUT replaces the whole profile, and the first pull request is write-once
description:
Three rules from ADR-0018 that a PATCH-shaped implementation would break quietly.

FIRST, THE REPLACE. The endpoint is a PUT and not a PATCH, because a profile form submits every field it shows, so a full replace says what happened. The test is the one a merge passes by accident in every other case — set two flags, then submit a body with all four false. A merge leaves a flag set that somebody had just cleared and answers 200 as though it had not: the screen says they are not open to internships while the index says they are, and the only symptom is mail they never agreed to hear.

The country and the self-reported years clear the same way. An empty country stores NULL rather than leaving the previous one standing, which matters because current_country is matched against a role's eligible countries — a stale one puts somebody in front of roles in a country they have left. office_yoe returns to null, because not stated is not zero years.

SECOND, WRITE-ONCE (decision 7, as amended). first_pr_url is asked rather than derived — a first contribution is often years old in a repository nobody claimed here, and a claim is five PRs somebody chose as their BEST, not their earliest — and once recorded it cannot be changed. A field revisable downward whenever it suited would be worth nothing to the hirer reading it. A second, DIFFERENT value is refused with a readable error rather than silently overruled, because a client that sent a new value and got a 200 would show it back and believe it had saved. latest_pr_url is editable in the same request, because it goes stale by definition.

Re-sending the SAME first PR is accepted, which is what a form showing the field does on every save. That matters to a client: since this is a replace, it has to keep echoing the value it was given.

THIRD, needs_attention (amendment 2) is about having been ASKED, not about the answer. The all-false step is the proof: every flag off, matchable false, needs_attention false. 'I am not open to any of these right now' is a real answer somebody may mean, and nobody should be nagged about a decision they made.

Every refusal also asserts the table, because the interesting half of a refusal is what it did NOT write: the 409 arrives carrying four flags and a country, and none of them may land.

steps._step: The full form, as the screen submits it. Two flags on, two off, and both pull requests stated for the first time.

expect._note: office_yoe 4 beside a first PR from years earlier: two different facts about the same person, and the pair is the point — somebody with eight years of open source and one of employment is a specific person a hirer wants to be able to see. needs_attention goes false the moment she answers.

steps._step: Read back. What the write returned is what a later read returns, which is not free: the write answers from a re-read, so a column the upsert forgot would show up here rather than after a deploy.
SHE CLEARS EVERYTHING SHE IS ALLOWED TO CLEAR, and moves her latest PR on. The same first PR is echoed back, which is what a replace requires of a client.

expect._note: THE STEP A MERGE FAILS. All four flags are false, so she is unmatchable again despite a live window — and needs_attention is still FALSE, because she has answered. That pair is amendment 2: being unmatchable is not a reason to prompt somebody, only never having been asked is.

user_work_preferences._note: Still ONE row — the upsert updated rather than inserting a second — and every flag is false in the TABLE, not merely in the response. The country is NULL rather than two blank characters.

steps._step: A DIFFERENT FIRST PULL REQUEST. Refused by name, not accepted with the field quietly ignored.

expect._note: 409 rather than 200: a contributor who revised their start date and got an OK would go on believing they had, and the date a hirer reads would disagree with the one they typed. The repository coalesces as well, so the guarantee survives a caller who forgets to check — but a caller has to be TOLD, and only this layer can tell them.

user_work_preferences._note: THE WHOLE REQUEST DID NOTHING. open_to_remote is still false and the country is still NULL, so the four legal fields the same body carried did not land alongside the refused one. A partial write here would be the worst outcome: a profile half in the state somebody asked for.

steps._step: And the read confirms it. A 409 that had written the flags would be invisible from the response that refused it.

THE SAME first PR, with everything else moving. Accepted — the rule is 'cannot be CHANGED', not 'cannot be sent again', and a client submitting the form it was given must not be punished for echoing a value it is not allowed to alter.

user_work_preferences._note: latest_pr_url moved and first_pr_url did not. Editable and write-once, in one request.

steps._step: A BODY FROM A CLIENT BUILT AGAINST THE EARLIER DRAFT, which still thinks it can state an open-source-years figure. Decision 7 was amended precisely because that number was the wrong fact stated confidently, so the field has to be refused rather than accepted and dropped.

expect._note: 400 and not 200-with-the-field-dropped, the same reading as the two approved fixtures that pin a DisallowUnknownFields refusal: a caller that believes it saved twelve years would go on believing it. Decoding fails before any service runs, so nothing is written either.

steps._step: FREELANCE PERSISTS LIKE ANY OTHER PREFERENCE. It used to live on availability_status, so nothing here ever asserted it reaching this table. The whole point of moving it is that it is no longer special.
